# 1. Load packages and NHANES datasets

This analysis uses NHANES 2017–2018 data to examine the association between urinary 3-PBA and serum AMH concentrations among women aged 20-44 years.

```{r}
library(haven)
library(survey)
library(ggplot2)
library(tidyr)
```

## Download NHANES datasets directly from website
```{r}
# NHANES 2017-2018 data location
base <- "https://wwwn.cdc.gov/Nchs/Data/Nhanes/Public/2017/DataFiles/"

# Download and organize the seven datasets
nhanes <- list(
  pba = read_xpt(paste0(base, "UPHOPM_J.xpt")),
  amh = read_xpt(paste0(base, "SSTST_J.xpt")),
  demo = read_xpt(paste0(base, "DEMO_J.xpt")),
  bmi = read_xpt(paste0(base, "BMX_J.xpt")),
  creatinine = read_xpt(paste0(base, "ALB_CR_J.xpt")),
  smoking = read_xpt(paste0(base, "SMQ_J.xpt")),
  hormones = read_xpt(paste0(base, "RHQ_J.xpt")))

# Confirm which datasets loaded
names(nhanes)
```

# 2. Merge datasets and select variables

The NHANES datasets will be merged using SEQN, the unique participant identification number. Only variables needed for the study will be retained.

```{r}
# Select demographic variables
data <- nhanes$demo[, c(
  "SEQN", "RIAGENDR", "RIDAGEYR", "RIDEXPRG",
  "RIDRETH3", "DMDEDUC2", "INDFMPIR",
  "SDMVSTRA", "SDMVPSU")]

# Merge exposure and outcome
data <- merge(data, nhanes$pba[, c("SEQN", "URXOPM", "WTSB2YR")],
              by = "SEQN", all.x = TRUE)

data <- merge(data, nhanes$amh[, c("SEQN", "SSTAMH")],
              by = "SEQN", all.x = TRUE)

# Merge additional covariates and descriptive variables
data <- merge(data, nhanes$bmi[, c("SEQN", "BMXBMI")],
              by = "SEQN", all.x = TRUE)

data <- merge(data, nhanes$creatinine[, c("SEQN", "URXUCR")],
              by = "SEQN", all.x = TRUE)

data <- merge(data, nhanes$smoking[, c("SEQN", "SMQ020")],
              by = "SEQN", all.x = TRUE)

data <- merge(data, nhanes$hormones[, c("SEQN", "RHQ420")],
              by = "SEQN", all.x = TRUE)

# Check the dimensions of the combined dataset
dim(data)
```

# 3. Apply eligibility criteria and document exclusions

The study population consists of nonpregnant women aged 20-44 years with available urinary 3-PBA and serum AMH measurements. Participant counts are recorded at each stage of selection. 

Women whose pregnancy status could not be ascertained are excluded along with those confirmed pregnant.

```{r}
# Check pregnancy status among women aged 20–44
table(
  data$RIDEXPRG[data$RIAGENDR == 2 &
                  data$RIDAGEYR >= 20 &
                  data$RIDAGEYR <= 44],
  useNA = "always")
```
## Of the 9,254 NHANES participants, 1,110 were women aged 20-44 years. After restricting the sample to confirmed nonpregnant women, 966 remained. Of these, 253 had available measurements for both urinary 3-PBA and serum AMH and were included in the eligible study sample.

```{r}
# Define inclusion criteria step by step
# Identify female participants (RIAGENDR = 2 means female)
female <- data$RIAGENDR == 2

# Among females, identify those aged 20 through 44 years (inclusive)
age <- female & data$RIDAGEYR >= 20 & data$RIDAGEYR <= 44

# Among females aged 20–44, identify those confirmed as not pregnant (RIDEXPRG = 2)
nonpregnant <- age & data$RIDEXPRG == 2

# Among eligible nonpregnant women, identify those with both biomarker measurements available
biomarkers <- nonpregnant & !is.na(data$URXOPM) & !is.na(data$SSTAMH)

# Count participants at each stage
flow <- data.frame(
  Stage = c(
    "All NHANES participants",
    "Female participants",
    "Women aged 20-44",
    "Confirmed nonpregnant",
    "Available 3-PBA and AMH"
  ),
  N = c(
    nrow(data),
    sum(female, na.rm = TRUE),
    sum(age, na.rm = TRUE),
    sum(nonpregnant, na.rm = TRUE),
    sum(biomarkers, na.rm = TRUE)))

# Create the eligible study sample
sample <- subset(
  data,
  RIAGENDR == 2 &
    RIDAGEYR >= 20 &
    RIDAGEYR <= 44 &
    RIDEXPRG == 2 &
    !is.na(URXOPM) &
    !is.na(SSTAMH))

# Display participant counts
flow
```

# 4. Assess missing data and variable coding

Missing values are assessed among eligible participants before selecting covariates for regression models.
```{r}
# Count missing values for each variable in the eligible sample
colSums(is.na(sample))
```
# Among the 253 eligible participants, income-to-poverty ratio (PIR) was missing for 30 women, BMI was missing for one woman, and birth control pill history was missing for 18 women. Because PIR was included as a covariate in the regression models, the primary regression analysis was restricted to 223 complete cases. BMI and birth control pill history were used for descriptive purposes only and were not included in the regression models.

## Check variable coding and biomarker distributions

```{r}
# Examine response codes before recoding variables
table(sample$SMQ020, useNA = "always")
table(sample$RHQ420, useNA = "always")
table(sample$DMDEDUC2, useNA = "always")

# Summarize the exposure and outcome distributions
summary(sample$URXOPM)
summary(sample$SSTAMH)

# Check whether either variable contains zero or negative values
sum(sample$URXOPM <= 0, na.rm = TRUE)
sum(sample$SSTAMH <= 0, na.rm = TRUE)
```
# Among 253 women, urinary 3-PBA (µg/L) had an unweighted median of 0.75 (IQR 0.35–1.60), mean of 2.55, and maximum of 110. Serum AMH (ng/mL) had an unweighted median of 2.39 (IQR 1.07–4.07), mean of 2.89, and maximum of 22.29. Both distributions were right-skewed, and neither contained nonpositive values.


## Visualize biomarker distributions

Histograms were used to visually examine the distributions of urinary 3-PBA and serum AMH before selecting transformations for regression analysis.

```{r analysis-6}
# Urinary 3-PBA distribution
ggplot(sample, aes(x = URXOPM)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 25, fill = "#4C78A8", color = "white") +
  labs(
    title = "Distribution of Urinary 3-PBA",
    x = "Urinary 3-PBA (µg/L)",
    y = "Count"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()

# Serum AMH distribution
ggplot(sample, aes(x = SSTAMH)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 25, fill = "#E08B65", color = "white") +
  labs(
    title = "Distribution of Serum AMH",
    x = "Serum AMH (ng/mL)",
    y = "Count"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

# 5. Specify NHANES survey design

NHANES uses a complex, multistage sampling design. The analysis will account for environmental subsample weights, sampling strata, and primary sampling units (PSU).
```{r}
# Check the laboratory subsample weights
summary(sample$WTSB2YR)

# Count missing weights
sum(is.na(sample$WTSB2YR))

# Count zero or negative weights
sum(sample$WTSB2YR <= 0, na.rm = TRUE)
```
```{r}
# Define the design among participants with valid lab weights
design <- svydesign(
  ids = ~SDMVPSU,
  strata = ~SDMVSTRA,
  weights = ~WTSB2YR,
  nest = TRUE,
  data = subset(data, !is.na(WTSB2YR) & WTSB2YR > 0))

# Restrict to eligible study population
design <- subset(
  design,
  RIAGENDR == 2 &
    RIDAGEYR >= 20 &
    RIDAGEYR <= 44 &
    RIDEXPRG == 2 &
    !is.na(URXOPM) &
    !is.na(SSTAMH))

# Verify the eligible sample size
nrow(design$variables)
```

# 6. Generate Table 1 and descriptive statistics
Table 1 describes the 253 eligible women with urinary 3-PBA and serum AMH measurements. Continuous characteristics are summarized using survey-weighted means or medians, and categorical characteristics using unweighted counts and survey-weighted percentages. Smoking and birth control pill history are descriptive variables, not regression covariates.

```{r}
# Format survey-weighted means and standard errors
mean_se <- function(variable) {
  x <- svymean(as.formula(paste0("~", variable)),
               design, na.rm = TRUE)
  sprintf("%.2f (%.2f)", coef(x)[1], SE(x)[1])
}

# Format survey-weighted median and interquartile range
median_iqr <- function(variable) {
  x <- svyquantile(
    as.formula(paste0("~", variable)),
    design,
    quantiles = c(0.25, 0.50, 0.75),
    na.rm = TRUE,
    ci = FALSE
  )
  q <- as.numeric(coef(x))
  sprintf("%.2f (%.2f–%.2f)", q[2], q[1], q[3])}

# Format unweighted count and survey-weighted percentage
category_result <- function(variable, code) {
  n <- sum(sample[[variable]] == code, na.rm = TRUE)
  weighted <- svytable(
    as.formula(paste0("~", variable)), design
  )
  pct <- 100 * as.numeric(weighted[as.character(code)]) /
    sum(weighted)
  sprintf("%d (%.1f%%)", n, pct)}

# Race/ethnicity categories in NHANES
race_codes <- c(1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 7)
race_labels <- c(
  "  Mexican American",
  "  Other Hispanic",
  "  Non-Hispanic White",
  "  Non-Hispanic Black",
  "  Non-Hispanic Asian",
  "  Other / Multiracial")

# Education categories in NHANES
education_codes <- 1:5
education_labels <- c(
  "  Less than 9th grade",
  "  9th–11th grade",
  "  High school graduate / GED",
  "  Some college / Associate degree",
  "  College graduate or above")

# Assemble Table 1
table1 <- data.frame(
  Characteristic = c(
    "Age (years), mean (SE)",
    "BMI (kg/m²), mean (SE)",
    "Urinary 3-PBA (µg/L), median (Q1–Q3)",
    "Serum AMH (ng/mL), median (Q1–Q3)",
    "Urinary creatinine (mg/dL), median (Q1–Q3)",
    "Income-to-poverty ratio, mean (SE)",
    "Race/ethnicity, n (weighted %)",
    race_labels,
    "Education, n (weighted %)",
    education_labels,
    "Ever smoked ≥100 cigarettes, Yes, n (weighted %)",
    "Ever used birth control pills, Yes, n (weighted %)"
  ),
  Result = c(
    mean_se("RIDAGEYR"),
    mean_se("BMXBMI"),
    median_iqr("URXOPM"),
    median_iqr("SSTAMH"),
    median_iqr("URXUCR"),
    mean_se("INDFMPIR"),
    "",
    sapply(race_codes, function(x)
      category_result("RIDRETH3", x)),
    "",
    sapply(education_codes, function(x)
      category_result("DMDEDUC2", x)),
    category_result("SMQ020", 1),
    category_result("RHQ420", 1)
  )
)

knitr::kable(
  table1,
  col.names = c("Characteristic", "Eligible sample (N = 253)"),
  caption = "Table 1. Characteristics of eligible women, NHANES 2017–2018"
)
```

## 7. Visualize the exposure–outcome relationship

An unweighted scatterplot was used to examine the relationship between urinary 3-PBA and serum AMH among the 253 eligible participants. Because urinary 3-PBA was right-skewed, it was natural-log transformed to improve visualization and match the exposure transformation used in the regression models. Serum AMH was retained on its original scale (ng/mL) for interpretation.

```{r}
ggplot(sample, aes(x = log(URXOPM), y = SSTAMH)) +
  geom_point(color = "#4C78A8", alpha = 0.5) +
  labs(
    title = "Log urinary 3-PBA and serum AMH",
    x = "log (urinary 3-PBA)",
    y = "Serum AMH (ng/mL)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

The scatterplot shows substantial variability in serum AMH across log-transformed urinary 3-PBA concentrations, without a clear visual linear relationship. Several observations have relatively high AMH concentrations, which will be considered during regression diagnostics.

## 8. Urine-dilution-adjusted and multivariable regression models

I fitted two survey-weighted linear regression models to examine the association between natural-log-transformed urinary 3-PBA and serum AMH. The first adjusted for urinary creatinine, while the primary model additionally adjusted for age and family income-to-poverty ratio (PIR), guided by the literature-informed DAG. Both models used the same complete-case sample and accounted for NHANES environmental subsample weights, strata, and primary sampling units.

```{r}
# Create log-transformed urinary 3-PBA within the survey design
design <- update(design, log_pba = log(URXOPM))

# Restrict both models to participants with complete covariate data
design_models <- subset(
  design,
  !is.na(INDFMPIR) & !is.na(URXUCR) & !is.na(RIDAGEYR))

# Model 1: Exposure association, adjusted for urine dilution
model_unadjusted <- svyglm(
  SSTAMH ~ log_pba + URXUCR,
  design = design_models)

# Model 2: Additionally adjusted for DAG-selected confounders
model_adjusted <- svyglm(
  SSTAMH ~ log_pba + URXUCR + RIDAGEYR + INDFMPIR,
  design = design_models)

# Display regression results
summary(model_unadjusted)
summary(model_adjusted)
confint(model_adjusted)["log_pba", ]

# Check the sample size used in both models
nrow(design_models$variables)
```
# In the urinary creatinine-adjusted model, the association between natural-log-transformed urinary 3-PBA and serum AMH was negative but not statistically significant (β = −0.098; p = 0.569). After additional adjustment for age and income-to-poverty ratio, the estimated association remained negative and statistically nonsignificant (β = −0.046; 95% CI: −0.376 to 0.283; p = 0.763). Age was negatively associated with serum AMH in the primary adjusted model (β = −0.152; p = 0.003). These findings did not provide statistically significant evidence of an association between urinary 3-PBA and serum AMH in this sample.

## 9. Effect modification by age

I examined whether age modified the association between urinary 3-PBA and serum AMH by including an interaction term between log-transformed 3-PBA and continuous age in the survey-weighted adjusted model. Statistical significance of the interaction was assessed using the survey-design-adjusted Wald t-test.

```{r}
# Test whether age modifies the association
model_interaction <- svyglm(
  SSTAMH ~ log_pba * RIDAGEYR + URXUCR + INDFMPIR,
  design = design_models)

# View the regression results
summary(model_interaction)

# Confidence interval for the interaction
confint(model_interaction)["log_pba:RIDAGEYR", ]
```
# The interaction between natural-log-transformed urinary 3-PBA and continuous age was not statistically significant (β = −0.0018; 95% CI: −0.0376 to 0.0341; p = 0.915). This analysis did not provide statistical evidence that age modified the association between urinary 3-PBA and serum AMH among women aged 20–44 years.


## 10. Regression diagnostics
### 10.1 Residuals versus fitted values
```{r}
diagnostic_data <- data.frame(
  fitted = fitted(model_adjusted),
  residuals = residuals(model_adjusted))

ggplot(diagnostic_data, aes(x = fitted, y = residuals)) +
  geom_point(color = "#4C78A8", alpha = 0.5) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, color = "#E45756",
             linewidth = 1, linetype = "dashed") +
  labs(
    title = "Residuals versus fitted values",
    x = "Fitted serum AMH (ng/mL)",
    y = "Residuals (ng/mL)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```
The residuals-versus-fitted plot shows a funnel-shaped pattern, with residual variability increasing at higher fitted AMH values, suggesting a violation of the constant variance assumption (heteroscedasticity) in the linear regression model.

### 10.2 Normal Q–Q plot
```{r}
ggplot(
  data.frame(residuals = residuals(model_adjusted)),
  aes(sample = residuals)
) +
  stat_qq(color = "#4C78A8", alpha = 0.5) +
  stat_qq_line(color = "#E45756", linewidth = 1) +
  labs(
    title = "Normal Q-Q plot of adjusted model residuals",
    x = "Theoretical quantiles",
    y = "Sample quantiles"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```
The normal Q–Q plot shows substantial deviations from the reference line in the upper tail, suggesting a violation of the normality assumption, with right-skewed residuals and several large positive outliers.

### 10.3 Residuals versus continuous predictors

```{r}
# Extract variables used in the fitted model
diagnostic_data2 <- data.frame(
  log_pba = model.frame(model_adjusted)$log_pba,
  age = model.frame(model_adjusted)$RIDAGEYR,
  residuals = residuals(model_adjusted)
)

# Reshape the data for plotting
diagnostic_long <- tidyr::pivot_longer(
  diagnostic_data2,
  cols = c(log_pba, age),
  names_to = "variable",
  values_to = "value"
)

ggplot(diagnostic_long, aes(x = value, y = residuals)) +
  geom_point(color = "#4C78A8", alpha = 0.5) +
  geom_hline(
    yintercept = 0,
    color = "#E45756",
    linetype = "dashed"
  ) +
  facet_wrap(~ variable, scales = "free_x") +
  labs(
    title = "Residuals versus model predictors",
    x = "Predictor value",
    y = "Residuals (ng/mL)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```
Residuals plotted against age and log-transformed urinary 3-PBA showed no clear systematic patterns, although several large positive residuals were observed.

### 10.4 Approximate influence screening

# Cook’s distance and DFBETAs

```{r}
# Weighted linear model for influence screening
diagnostic_model <- lm(
  SSTAMH ~ log_pba + URXUCR + RIDAGEYR + INDFMPIR,
  data = design_models$variables,
  weights = WTSB2YR)

# Cook's distance
cooks <- cooks.distance(diagnostic_model)

# DFBETAs for the 3-PBA coefficient
pba_dfbetas <- dfbetas(diagnostic_model)[, "log_pba"]

# Identify potentially influential observations
influential <- which(
  abs(pba_dfbetas) > 2 / sqrt(length(pba_dfbetas)))

# Number of flagged observations
length(influential)
```


### 10.5 Exploratory influence sensitivity check

The primary analysis retains all eligible observations. The following exploratory comparison assesses how the exposure coefficient changes when the eight observations flagged by the additional DFBETA screen are temporarily excluded.

```{r}
# Identify the participants flagged by DFBETAs
flagged_ids <- design_models$variables$SEQN[influential]

# Fit the sensitivity model excluding flagged participants
model_sensitivity <- svyglm(
  SSTAMH ~ log_pba + URXUCR + RIDAGEYR + INDFMPIR,
  design = subset(design_models, !(SEQN %in% flagged_ids)))

# View regression results
summary(model_sensitivity)

# Compare the 3-PBA coefficients
coef(model_adjusted)["log_pba"]
coef(model_sensitivity)["log_pba"]

# Confidence interval for the sensitivity estimate
confint(model_sensitivity)["log_pba", ]
```
# After excluding the eight potentially influential observations, the estimated association between urinary 3-PBA and serum AMH became somewhat more negative (β = −0.097; 95% CI: −0.293 - 0.099; p = 0.298). However, the association remained statistically nonsignificant. Therefore, this exploratory sensitivity analysis did not change the overall conclusion of the primary analysis.

## 11. Sensitivity analysis: Race/ethnicity adjustment

I conducted a sensitivity analysis additionally adjusting for race/ethnicity to assess whether the estimated association between urinary 3-PBA and serum AMH was sensitive to this adjustment. Race/ethnicity was treated as a categorical variable.

```{r}
# Fit sensitivity model with additional race/ethnicity adjustment
model_ethnicity <- svyglm(
  SSTAMH ~ log_pba + URXUCR + RIDAGEYR + INDFMPIR +
    factor(RIDRETH3),
  design = design_models)

# View the full regression results
summary(model_ethnicity)

# Compare the 3-PBA coefficients
coef(model_adjusted)["log_pba"]
coef(model_ethnicity)["log_pba"]

# Confidence interval for the sensitivity estimate
confint(model_ethnicity)["log_pba", ]
```
# After additional adjustment for race/ethnicity, the estimated association between urinary 3-PBA and serum AMH remained negative and statistically nonsignificant (β = −0.022; 95% CI: −0.419 - 0.376; p = 0.899). 


## 12. Conclusion
# In this cross-sectional analysis of NHANES 2017-2018 data, urinary 3-PBA was not significantly associated with serum AMH among nonpregnant women aged 20-44 years after adjustment for urinary creatinine, age, and income-to-poverty ratio. There was no statistically significant evidence of effect modification by age, and sensitivity analyses did not change the overall conclusion.

# These findings should be interpreted cautiously because of the cross-sectional study design, relatively small regression sample, and limitations identified during regression diagnostics. Future longitudinal studies may help clarify the relationship between pyrethroid exposure and ovarian reserve.
